doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
title: Instrumentation of the I Want to Live! score
summary: Mandel says he chose his jazz orchestra with four French horns and unusual winds because they matched the sounds in his head, creating the first all-jazz film score.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: So as far as the orchestral score that you did, my description of it would be a jazz orchestra augmented by certain orchestral instruments like E-flat clarinet, contrabassoon, contrabass clarinet that were pretty unorthodox and still are.
Four French horns.
Yeah.
Yeah it was a very large-sized jazz orchestra.
You had total freedom as far as picking instrumentation?
I sure did.
Why did you decide on that particular combination of instruments, what was the attraction for you there?

They made the sounds that I heard in my head in conjunction with this picture. So, I never ever decide on a bunch of instruments ahead of time and then try to write music to fit it, instead I try to make the noises I hear in my head. When I say noises you know, music and…
Sure.
I think in terms of sound and whatever instruments that happens to be, that's what I end up getting.
There was one…

I didn't want to use strings in this, so the closest thing I could get would've been a combination between a jazz orchestra and a wind band, so that's what I ended up using. But it was a jazz driven score, in fact it really was the first all jazz score that ever was for movies. You know different people used jazz in patches in movies up ‘til then but when they got into real heavy emotional scenes they’d almost always revert to traditional underscore.
Like the…
With the symphonic type, regular symphonic type orchestra set up.
Yeah, I can think of two instances of what you describe like that Alex North score for Streetcar Named Desire.
Right.
And Elmer Bernstein’s Man with the Golden Arm.
Exactly, um-hm.
Yeah, but you definitely, you took it beyond that…
Even Leith Stevens in, The Wild One.
That Shorty Rogers worked on.
Yeah but Leith wrote the music.
